## Mapped: The World’s Top Financial Centers in 2025

This was originally posted on our Voronoi app. Download the app for free on iOS or Android and discover incredible data-driven charts from a variety of trusted sources.

### Key Takeaways

- The 37th edition of the Global Financial Centres Index (GFCI 37) ranks the competitiveness of 119 financial hubs 
- Little has changed at the top of the index, with New York, London, and Hong Kong continuing their long-standing dominance

Financial centers are a core pillar of the modern economy, channeling capital, facilitating trade, and driving innovation across the world.

In this graphic, we visualized the world’s top 40 most competitive financial centers, using data from the 37th edition of the Global Financial Centres Index (GFCI 37).

## Data & Methodology

The GFCI 37 was compiled using 140 quantitative measures from sources like the World Bank, OECD, and UN. 

These measures are combined with assessments collected by respondents to the GFCI online questionnaire. In total, the GFCI 37 used 31,314 assessments from 4,946 respondents.

#### Areas of Competitiveness

The quantitative factors used in the GFCI model are grouped into five areas of competitiveness: 

Business environment: Transparency and stability of systems, regulatory complexity

Human capital: Access to skill professionals, investment in education

Infrastructure: Quality of physical and digital infrastructure

Financial sector development: Accessibility to clients, development of digital solutions

Reputation: Trustworthiness of legal and regulatory systems

## Regional Insights

We’ve summarized the main highlights from each GFCI region below.

#### North America

North America has four centers in the top 10: New York, San Francisco, Chicago, and Los Angeles. The most improved within North America are Miami and Vancouver, which both climbed over 10 places in the ranking.

#### Western Europe

London is the region’s dominant center, with seven other cities featuring in the top 20. The average rating across Western Europe increased by 2.14%.

#### Asia Pacific

Asia Pacific has six centers in the top 20, with four belonging to China (Hong Kong SAR, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Beijing). Looking elsewhere, Hangzhou, New Delhi, Kuala Lumpur, Ho Chi Minh City, and Manila all rose six or more places.

#### Middle East & Africa

The region’s leading centers are Dubai and Abu Dhabi, with Dubai climbing four places to 12th in GFCI 37. Meanwhile, Tel Aviv, Kuwait City, and Johannesburg each fell more than 10 places.

#### Latin America & The Caribbean

São Paulo rose seven places this year, making it the leading financial center in the region. 

## How the World’s 30 Largest Banks Rank in 2026

### Key Takeaways

- China is home to the world’s four largest banks by total assets.
- JPMorgan Chase ($4.42 trillion) is the world’s largest bank outside China.
- France’s BNP Paribas ($3.28 trillion) is Europe’s largest bank by total assets.

America’s biggest bank ranks only fifth globally, highlighting the enormous scale of China’s banking system.

This graphic ranks the world’s 30 largest banks using S&P Global Market Intelligence’s April 2026 ranking, based primarily on year-end 2025 financial statements. Total assets include loans, investments, and cash, with banks grouped by the country of their headquarters.

## China’s Megabanks Outsize Wall Street

Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) leads with $7.65 trillion in assets, roughly 73% more than JPMorgan Chase’s $4.42 trillion.

Together, China’s Big Four banks hold more than $26 trillion in assets, nearly twice the combined total of America’s five largest banks: JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, and Goldman Sachs.

- Three U.S. companies account for 93.4% of outstanding credit ratings reported to U.S. regulators.
- S&P Global Ratings leads the market with a 49.6% share, followed by Moody’s and Fitch.
- Credit ratings can influence how much governments and companies pay to borrow money.

A few letters beside a bond can influence how much a company pays to borrow money from investors. Behind those grades is an industry dominated by just three firms: S&P Global Ratings, Moody’s, and Fitch.

This graphic shows the share of outstanding credit ratings reported by agencies registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) as of the end of 2024. These ratings assess the ability of companies, governments, and other borrowers to repay their debts.

## The Big Three Rating Agencies

S&P, Moody’s, and Fitch together account for 93.4% of outstanding ratings, leaving just 6.6% for seven smaller competitors. S&P (Standard & Poor’s) alone holds nearly half the market.

Their dominance has proved remarkably durable. In 2007, the Big Three held a combined 98.8% share. Smaller competitors have gained ground since then, particularly Morningstar DBRS, but the industry’s balance of power has changed only gradually.

For borrowers, these assessments have financial consequences. Bonds rated below investment grade, commonly known as junk bonds, typically offer higher yields to compensate investors for greater default risk. For governments and large corporations borrowing billions of dollars, even a small increase in interest rates can translate into substantial additional costs.

The influence of the Big Three extends to the U.S. government. S&P stripped the country of its highest-grade credit rating in 2011, Fitch followed in 2023, and Moody’s lowered its rating from Aaa to Aa1 in May 2025. The agencies cited concerns including persistent fiscal deficits, rising debt burdens, and political gridlock.

## Why Rivals Struggle to Break In

Challenging the Big Three requires more than producing good research. Many pension funds and other institutional investors operate under investment rules that specify which rating agencies they can rely on. Historically, those agencies have often been S&P, Moody’s, and Fitch, giving borrowers a strong reason to seek their ratings.

Bond indexes reinforce that advantage. Some require ratings from specified agencies before a bond can qualify for inclusion. These requirements matter because funds tracking the indexes invest in the bonds they contain, creating another incentive for borrowers to use established rating agencies.

Together, these practices help explain why the market is difficult to disrupt. Borrowers seek ratings that investors already accept, while investors continue relying on familiar providers. A newcomer must win recognition on both sides, not simply offer a cheaper service.

## Paid by the Borrowers They Rate

One of the industry’s most persistent controversies is how credit rating agencies make money. The largest firms generally collect fees from the borrowers whose creditworthiness they assess, creating a potential conflict of interest. Investors expect independent judgments, but the paying clients benefit from favorable ratings.

This arrangement matters because ratings influence investment decisions across a global bond market worth roughly $160 trillion.

Those tensions came into focus after the 2008 financial crisis. S&P agreed to a $1.375 billion settlement in 2015, while Moody’s reached an $864 million settlement in 2017, resolving allegations involving their ratings of mortgage-related investments before the crisis.

Post-crisis reforms strengthened safeguards intended to separate credit analysis from sales activities and reduce commercial pressure on ratings decisions. With so much of the market relying on three agencies, the independence of those judgments matters far beyond the firms themselves.
